title: Laptops & mobile devices
monthTitle: PC Hardware & How Computers Work (A+ Core 1)
summary: Learn how laptops differ from desktops, identify the parts that make them portable, and understand power, batteries, docking, and the common faults you will support on a helpdesk.
objectives: Explain the trade-offs between laptops and desktops (portability, power, repairability)
Identify laptop-specific parts: Li-ion battery, SODIMM RAM, M.2 storage, integrated display, Fn keys, touchpad
Describe how laptops are powered and charged, including AC adapters and USB-C Power Delivery
Explain what a docking station does and when to use one
Compare mobile device types: smartphones, tablets, and 2-in-1s
Diagnose common laptop issues such as overheating, won't charge, and a dim screen

quiz.q: Which RAM form factor is designed for laptops because it is physically smaller than a desktop module?
quiz.why: SODIMM (Small Outline DIMM) is the compact memory module used in laptops; full-size DIMMs are used in desktops and would not fit a laptop's tight chassis.

quiz.q: A user's laptop is plugged in but the battery says "plugged in, not charging" and the device feels very hot. What is the most likely first thing to check?
options: Airflow and vents — overheating can pause charging, and blocked vents cause it
quiz.why: Heat and blocked vents are common, cheap-to-fix causes; dust-clogged fans and vents make a laptop run hot and can stop the battery charging. Always check the simple, physical things first.

quiz.q: What does USB-C Power Delivery (PD) let a laptop do?
options: Charge over the same USB-C cable that also carries data and video
quiz.why: USB-C PD negotiates higher voltages and currents so a single USB-C cable can charge the laptop while also moving data and video, which is why many modern laptops charge from a USB-C dock or phone charger.

quiz.q: Why are laptops generally harder to repair and upgrade than desktops?
options: They run a different operating system
Parts are smaller, tightly packed, and often soldered to the board
quiz.why: To stay thin and light, laptops pack components tightly and increasingly solder RAM and storage to the motherboard, so upgrades and repairs are limited compared with a roomy, modular desktop.

quiz.q: What does the Fn (Function) key on a laptop keyboard do?
quiz.answer: It is a modifier key that, when held with another key (often the F1-F12 row), triggers a secondary action such as adjusting screen brightness, volume, Wi-Fi, or the external display.
quiz.why: Laptops cram many controls onto few keys, so Fn unlocks a second layer of hardware shortcuts printed on the keys, like brightness, volume, and toggling the touchpad or wireless.

quiz.q: Name one thing a user can do to look after a Li-ion laptop battery's long-term health.
quiz.answer: Avoid keeping it at extreme charge or heat — for example don't leave it constantly at 100% in a hot place; keeping it cool and roughly between 20% and 80% helps it last longer.
quiz.why: Lithium-ion batteries age faster under high heat and when held at very high or very low charge for long periods, so moderate charge levels and good cooling extend their useful life.

body_markdown:
## Laptop vs desktop: the trade-offs

A **laptop** packs a whole computer — screen, keyboard, trackpad, battery, and all the internals — into one portable shell. A **desktop** spreads those parts across a roomy case with separate monitor and keyboard. The difference is all about trade-offs.

- **Portability:** laptops win — you can carry them anywhere and run on battery.
- **Power & cooling:** desktops win — bigger cases mean faster parts and better airflow.
- **Repairability & upgrades:** desktops win — parts are modular and easy to swap, while laptops are tightly packed and increasingly have RAM and storage **soldered** to the board.

On a helpdesk you will support far more laptops than you might expect, so knowing their quirks matters.

## Laptop-specific parts

Laptops use shrunk-down versions of familiar components:

- **Battery** — a rechargeable **Lithium-ion (Li-ion)** pack that powers the laptop unplugged.
- **SODIMM RAM** — a **Small Outline DIMM**, the compact memory stick laptops use instead of full-size desktop DIMMs.
- **M.2 storage** — a small stick-shaped SSD that plugs flat onto the board, replacing bulky 2.5-inch drives.
- **Integrated display** — the screen is built in and connected by a delicate ribbon cable.
- **Function (Fn) key** — a modifier that unlocks a second layer of shortcuts (brightness, volume, Wi-Fi) printed on the keys.
- **Touchpad** — the built-in pointing surface that replaces a mouse.

## Power & charging

Most laptops charge from an **AC adapter** (the "power brick") that converts wall power to low-voltage DC. Each adapter supplies a specific wattage — too weak an adapter may run the laptop but not charge it.

Modern laptops increasingly charge over **USB-C Power Delivery (USB-C PD)**, where a single USB-C cable carries power, data, and video at once. That is why one charger can power a phone, tablet, or laptop.

A **docking station** turns a laptop into a desk setup: connect one cable and you instantly get power, monitors, wired network, and USB devices. Great for staff who roam but want a full workstation at their desk.

## Mobile devices

Beyond laptops you will support:

- **Smartphones** — pocket computers with cellular data and touchscreens.
- **Tablets** — larger touchscreens, often with optional keyboards.
- **2-in-1s** — laptops whose screens detach or fold back to act as a tablet.

These share laptop concerns: Li-ion batteries, limited repairability, and wireless connectivity.

## Battery health & common issues

Li-ion batteries age with **heat** and with sitting at very high or very low charge. Keep devices cool and avoid leaving them pinned at 100% in hot spots. Windows can produce a detailed battery report:

```powershell
powercfg /batteryreport
```

That saves an HTML file showing design capacity versus current full-charge capacity — a great way to prove a battery is worn out. You can also query the battery quickly:

```powershell
Get-CimInstance Win32_Battery
```

Common faults to recognise:

- **Overheating** — dust-clogged fans and vents; clean airflow and check it isn't on a soft surface.
- **Won't charge** — try a known-good adapter and cable, check the port for debris, and confirm it isn't simply too hot.
- **Dim screen** — check the brightness Fn keys first, then the power plan and display ribbon.

## Your task

On a Windows laptop, open PowerShell and run `powercfg /batteryreport`. Open the saved HTML file and find the **design capacity** and the **full charge capacity**. Write down both numbers and work out roughly how much battery health has been lost. Then run `Get-CimInstance Win32_Battery` and note the battery status.

slides.narration: Welcome to Lesson Seven. So far we've looked at the parts inside a desktop PC. Now we shrink everything down and look at laptops and mobile devices. By the end you'll know how a laptop differs from a desktop, the special parts that make it portable, how it charges, and the common faults you'll meet every single day on a helpdesk.

slides.title: Laptop vs desktop
bullets: Laptop: everything in one portable shell.
Desktop: roomy case, separate monitor and keyboard.
Laptops win on portability; desktops on power and repair.
You'll support more laptops than you expect.
slides.narration: Let's start with the big picture. A laptop packs the whole computer, screen, keyboard, trackpad, and battery, into one portable shell. A desktop spreads those parts across a roomy case. Laptops win on portability because you can carry them anywhere and run on battery. Desktops win on raw power, cooling, and how easy they are to repair and upgrade.

slides.title: Why laptops are harder to fix
bullets: Parts are smaller and tightly packed.
RAM and storage are often soldered to the board.
Thin-and-light designs limit upgrades.
Desktops stay modular and easy to swap.
slides.narration: Here's a key point for the helpdesk. To stay thin and light, laptops pack everything in very tightly, and more and more they solder the memory and storage straight onto the motherboard. That means upgrades and repairs are limited compared with a desktop, where parts are modular and you can simply swap them out. So always check what's actually replaceable before you promise a fix.

slides.title: Laptop-specific parts
bullets: Battery: rechargeable Lithium-ion pack.
SODIMM: the compact laptop RAM stick.
M.2: small stick-shaped SSD storage.
Integrated display connected by a ribbon cable.
slides.narration: Laptops use shrunk-down versions of parts you already know. The battery is a rechargeable Lithium-ion pack. The memory is a S O D I M M, that's a Small Outline dual inline memory module, smaller than a desktop stick. Storage is usually an M dot two solid state drive that lies flat on the board. And the display is built in, connected by a delicate ribbon cable.

slides.title: The Fn key and touchpad
bullets: Fn is a modifier key for a second layer of controls.
Hold Fn with F1-F12 for brightness, volume, Wi-Fi.
Touchpad replaces the mouse.
Many shortcuts are printed right on the keys.
slides.narration: Two controls are unique to laptops. The F n key, the function key, is a modifier. When you hold it with another key, usually the F one to F twelve row, it triggers a second action like brightness, volume, or turning Wi-Fi on and off. Look closely and you'll see those symbols printed on the keys. The touchpad is the built-in pointing surface that replaces a mouse.

slides.title: Power & charging
bullets: AC adapter (the 'brick') converts wall power to DC.
Wattage matters: a weak adapter may not charge.
USB-C PD: power, data, and video on one cable.
One USB-C charger can power phone, tablet, or laptop.
slides.narration: Most laptops charge from an A C adapter, the power brick, which converts wall power into low-voltage D C. Wattage matters: too weak an adapter might run the laptop but never charge it. Modern laptops also charge over U S B dash C P D, that's U S B dash C Power Delivery, where a single cable carries power, data, and video all at once. That's why one charger can power a phone, a tablet, or a laptop.

slides.title: Docking stations
bullets: One cable adds power, monitors, network, and USB.
Turns a roaming laptop into a full desk setup.
Great for hot-desking and office staff.
Often connects over USB-C or Thunderbolt.
slides.narration: A docking station is a brilliant tool for office users. The laptop connects with a single cable, and instantly you get power, external monitors, wired network, and all your U S B devices. It turns a roaming laptop into a full workstation the moment someone sits down. Most modern docks connect over U S B dash C or Thunderbolt.

slides.title: Mobile devices
bullets: Smartphones: pocket computers with cellular data.
Tablets: bigger touchscreens, optional keyboards.
2-in-1s: laptops whose screens fold or detach.
All share Li-ion batteries and limited repairability.
slides.narration: Beyond laptops you'll support mobile devices too. Smartphones are pocket computers with cellular data and a touchscreen. Tablets are larger touchscreens, often with an optional keyboard. And two-in-ones are laptops whose screens fold back or detach to become a tablet. They all share the same concerns: Lithium-ion batteries, limited repairability, and wireless connections.

slides.title: Battery health & a report
bullets: Li-ion ages with heat and extreme charge levels.

slides.narration: Lithium-ion batteries wear out faster with heat and when they sit at very high or very low charge for a long time. So keep devices cool and don't leave them pinned at one hundred percent in a hot spot. On Windows you can prove a battery is worn out: open PowerShell and run power c f g slash batteryreport, which saves an H T M L file comparing the original design capacity to the current full charge capacity. You can also run Get dash Cim Instance Win thirty-two Battery to check its status.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Laptops trade power and repair for portability.
Know SODIMM, M.2, Li-ion, Fn key, touchpad, USB-C PD.
Check heat, adapter, and Fn keys for common faults.
Task: run a battery report and read its capacity.
slides.narration: Let's recap. Laptops trade power and easy repair for portability. You should now recognise the S O D I M M, the M dot two drive, the Lithium-ion battery, the F n key, the touchpad, and U S B dash C P D charging. For common faults, check heat, try a known-good adapter, and check the brightness F n keys. Your task: on a Windows laptop, run power c f g slash batteryreport, open the file, and compare the design capacity to the full charge capacity to see how much health has been lost. Then run Get dash Cim Instance Win thirty-two Battery. See you in the next lesson.
